name: Han Purple
poem: An electric violet invented independently in Han China two thousand years ago — lost for centuries, rediscovered painted onto the Terracotta Army.

recipe.note: An electric violet — deep blue pushed toward red.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Han purple is one of the earliest synthetic pigments — invented in China two centuries BC, used for three hundred years, and then forgotten until the 1990s.

entries.title: The Terracotta Army
entries.meta: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang · c. 210 BC
entries.blurb: The 8,000 warriors were originally painted in vivid colours including Han purple — most pigment flaked off within hours of excavation, but micro-traces remain on robes.

entries.title: Han Pottery Figurines
entries.meta: Western Han tomb goods · 2nd c. BC
entries.blurb: Painted tomb figurines from Han burials at Yangling carry traces of Han purple on robes and sashes — the pigment was a status marker for the dead.

entries.title: Bronze Ritual Vessels
entries.blurb: Han purple appears as decorative pigment on bronze ritual vessels — applied over patinated bronze surfaces in geometric patterns, a colour the Han associated with the heavens.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Han purple, like its Mediterranean cousin Tyrian, was a colour of imperial rank — but worn on different bodies in a parallel system on the other side of the world.

entries.title: Han Court Robes
entries.blurb: Court protocol used dyed and pigment-decorated silks — Han purple appeared in trim and embroidery on the robes of high officials, never the everyday wardrobe.

entries.title: Buddhist Temple Banners
entries.blurb: Painted silk banners hung in Buddhist temples used Han purple for the robes of deities — a colour associated with transcendence and incense smoke.

entries.title: Wedding Ceremonies
entries.blurb: The Chinese wedding palette retains Han purple in trim and accents — paired with red for joy, the violet representing constancy and night-deep affection.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Han purple doesn't exist in nature — it had to be invented. But the deep violet hues it captures occur in living things, just rarely.

entries.title: Wisteria
entries.blurb: The native Chinese climbing vine produces racemes of exactly Han-purple flowers — a colour the Han potters may have been trying to imitate from their own gardens.

entries.title: Amethyst
entries.blurb: The same chemistry — barium copper silicates — that produces Han purple synthetically is loosely related to the natural processes giving amethyst its violet hue.

entries.title: Twilight on a Mountain
entries.blurb: The exact violet of mountains at the last moment of dusk is Han purple — a colour the Han may have invented precisely because they kept seeing it and couldn't reproduce it.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Han purple's modern life began in 1992 — when a chemist at the British Museum identified it on a Han bronze and triggered a wave of scientific interest.

entries.title: Quantum Properties
entries.blurb: Researchers discovered Han purple's crystal structure exhibits a rare "two-dimensional quantum state" near absolute zero — a 2,200-year-old pigment with applications in physics.

entries.title: Rediscovery
entries.blurb: The pigment's chemistry was reverse-engineered by a Swiss chemist studying Han bronzes — and within a decade the colour was being re-synthesised for conservation work.

entries.title: The Egyptian Cousin
entries.blurb: Han purple is chemically distinct but structurally similar to Egyptian Blue — both are calcium-copper silicates, both invented in the Bronze Age, neither aware of the other.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Han purple's name is modern — assigned by scholars when they rediscovered it. The Han themselves had different words.

entries.title: "Hàn Zǐ"
entries.blurb: Literally "Han purple" — the modern Chinese name, coined retrospectively after archaeological identification. The original Han term, if there was one, is lost.

entries.title: "Chinese Purple"
entries.blurb: The pigment's official scientific designation since 1992 — a placeholder Western name that distinguishes it from Egyptian Blue while acknowledging its origin.

entries.title: BaCuSi₂O₆
entries.blurb: Barium copper disilicate — the formula for Han purple. It tells you everything modern science knows, and nothing about why the Han wanted to make it.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Han purple is one of those rare colours whose symbolism keeps changing — imperial, then forgotten, then a quantum-physics curiosity.

entries.title: Imperial Authority
entries.blurb: Purple was the colour of the pole star and the supreme deity in Han cosmology — a colour that placed the emperor at the centre of a stable celestial order.

entries.title: Lost Knowledge
entries.blurb: Han purple's disappearance has become a parable in modern Chinese culture — a sophisticated technology lost to the centuries, only recovered by accident.

entries.title: Quantum Mystery
entries.blurb: The pigment now appears in popular-science books as an example of how ancient technologies sometimes anticipate modern physics by accident — a colour with strange depth.
